title: Checkpoint: The Nineteenth Century
objective: After this level you can connect the Romantics, the Gothic and the great realists into one century's story of the novel and the stage.
summary: From the Romantics and the Gothic to the realists and the modern stage: many of the century's great novels came in installments, and its writers looked both inward and outward.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: a century that read its novels in pieces.
cards.body: From London to Moscow, many of this chapter's stories first reached readers a part at a time. Here's the century in order, then the installment habit, then the two lenses its writers used.

cards.headline: The nineteenth century, story by story

events.label: The Pickwick Papers starts in monthly parts
Jane Eyre and Wuthering Heights appear
Flaubert is tried over Madame Bovary
A Doll's House ends with a slammed door

cards.headline: The installment century
cards.body: Dickens's Oliver Twist ran in Bentley's Miscellany from 1837 to 1839. Madame Bovary ran in the Revue de Paris in 1856, Crime and Punishment was serialized in 1866, and Anna Karenina came out in installments between 1875 and 1877. Across Europe, readers met the great novels of the age the way Dickens's readers did: a piece at a time, waiting for the next.

cards.headline: Two lenses: inward and outward
cards.body: Look back at the chapter. Some writers turned inward: Wordsworth's "spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings," Jane Eyre's first-person voice, Raskolnikov's torment. Others looked outward with care: realism's unembellished picture of ordinary life, Tolstoy's families inside a war, Ibsen's middle-class home. Keep both lenses handy when you read this century.

mascot.line: Don't memorize every date. Remember the two lenses: feeling from the inside, careful observation from the outside.

questions.prompt: How did readers first meet Madame Bovary, Crime and Punishment and Anna Karenina?

options.label: In installments, a part at a time
Read aloud by their authors on tour

questions.explanation: All three first appeared in installments: Madame Bovary in 1856, Crime and Punishment in 1866 and Anna Karenina from 1875 to 1877.

questions.prompt: Chapter recap: what set Frankenstein apart from the Gothic novels before it?

options.label: Its horror comes from a science experiment
It has no mystery or dread at all
It is set in a medieval monastery
options.rationale: Its hero works as a scientist.

options.label: It posed as a translated old manuscript

questions.explanation: Shelley dropped the Gothic's occult props and made her hero a scientist interested in galvanic electricity.

questions.prompt: What did Charlotte Brontë and Mary Ann Evans have in common as novelists?
questions.explanation: Charlotte Brontë published as Currer Bell and Mary Ann Evans as George Eliot.

questions.prompt: Back in Level 1, novels were said to show life as unheroic, even absurd. Which movement in this chapter made ordinary life its whole subject?

options.label: Science fiction
options.rationale: It asks what-if questions of science.

questions.explanation: Realism set out to depict ordinary contemporary life accurately and without embellishment.
